translation: He looks at the family, all girls; the mother with a baby at her breast is getting off the cart clumsily and the carter is hurrying her because the cart has to return to take others from the suburbs.
The bundle she had on her back falls and a few greyish rags and a single string of small, darkened beads spill out from it.
The woman picks them up, embarrassed, as if she had just revealed her deepest secrets to the world.
Deymowa passes her and suddenly a boy, maybe six or seven years old, runs up to her and looking at her with smiling eyes, very pleased with himself, says: "Praised be Jesus Christ!"
And she responds automatically, yet solemnly: "For ever and ever, amen.
And already her heart is gripped and tears fill her eyes.
She crouches next to the boy, grabbing him by the wrists, and he looks straight into her tear-filled eyes, still smiling, the little rascal.
The first buildings are springing up in front of them, suddenly, without warning.
It's clear that the fog alters the perception of distance, as Kasia herself seems surprised by this.
Suddenly it leaps, jerking the shafts, and if not for Roszko's decisive reaction and his whip, it would have tipped over the carriage.
Maybe Kaska was scared by the sparks flying from the forge, or by the unease of horses waiting for their turn to be shod.
Everywhere there's the nauseating scent of malt, permeating every item put out for sale.
You can fill up on it like bread.
There are a few small breweries in Babintsy, a suburb of Rohatyn; the satisfying smell spreads all over the area from there.
Many stalls sell beer here, and the better shops have both vodka and mead in stock, mainly trójniak.
The establishment of the Jewish merchant Wakszul offers wine, genuine Hungarian and genuine Rhenish, and a slightly sour variety that they bring all the way from Wallachia.
The most could be said about the Wolowski family, as it had grown to enormous proportions.
Almost all branches of this family were ennobled, some with the Buffalo coat of arms, others with the Helmets.
Undoubtedly, Franciszek, the son of Isaac Wołowski, the same man whom Father Chmielowski named Jeremiah, had a great career.
Born in 1786 in Brünn and raised in Offenbach, he became one of the foremost lawyers and legal scholars of his time.
Interestingly, when a proposal to grant Polish citizenship to Jews appeared in the Sejm, Franciszek as a member of parliament argued in his stirring speech that it was not yet time for such a step.
First, the Polish nation must fight for its independence, and then it will be time for social reforms.
All the Offenbach neophytes were buried in the city cemetery, which after several years began to interfere with the city's expansion plans and was closed down in 1866.
The bones of the people buried there were gathered and respectfully reburied in another place.
On this occasion, the skull of Jakub Frank was exhumed from the grave and, meticulously labeled as "the skull of a Jewish patriarch", ended up in the hands of the Offenbach city historian.
Many years later, under unknown circumstances, it made its way to Berlin, where it was subjected to detailed measurements and studies and deemed an example of the racial inferiority of Jews.
After the war, it disappeared without a trace, possibly destroyed in the wartime turmoil, disintegrated to dust, or still lying in the underground storage of some museum.
After Jakub's death, a time of great peace came for me.
My primary occupation became studying the merkava, to which were added our conversations with Jeruchim Dembowski, as we began living in the same room, bringing us closer together.

To him, Jeruchim, I also told about Chai Szor that she was the only woman whom I could love and did love since that beautiful moment when I got her for one night, which was when I came with news about Jakub to Rohatyn.
But above all, I loved Jacob.
They had been in Ivaniv since April.
If it weren't for the good Ivan's people, they would probably starve to death.
Ivan saved their lives and health, Bejla is now feeling better and no longer coughs as much.
Srol believes that once they are baptized, they will be as well off as Christians.
They will receive a piece of land, Bejla will have vegetables in the garden, and he, Srol, will weave rugs, because he does that well.
In their old age, when they have married off the girls, they would take them in.
These are all his dreams.
"Look, benefactor, Kaśka doesn't want to go," Roszko says glumly when the carriage stops.
Roszko gets off the goat and waves goodbye a few times with exaggerated motions.
Then he leaned over and peered into the fog, as if looking into water.
From under his festive red, though somewhat faded, greatcoat, a shirt is peeking out.
"I don't know where to go," he says.
How do you not know?
"But we are already on the Rohatyn road," says the surprised priest.
And yet!
He gets out of the pram and follows the servant, helplessly circumventing the carriage, straining his eyes into the whiteness.
They think they see something, but eyes that cannot latch onto anything start playing tricks on them.
How could something like this have happened to them!
It's like losing oneself in one's own pocket.
"Quiet!" suddenly says the priest, raising his finger and listening attentively.
And indeed, somewhere from the left, through the bundles of mist, a faint murmur of water can be heard.
Let's follow that noise.
The priest decides that the water is flowing.
Soon the priest relaxes in the carriage, stretches out his legs and lets his eyes wander over the sea of fog.
He immediately fell into travel contemplation, because one thinks best when in motion.

Slowly, reluctantly, the mechanism of his mind comes to life; gears and cogs engage, setting the drive wheels in motion just like in the clock he keeps in his rectory hallway that was bought in Lviv; he paid dearly for it.
The ding-dong will sound any moment now.
He begins to wonder if the world hasn't emerged from such a fog.
After all, the Jewish historian Josephus maintains that the world was created in autumn, during the autumnal equinox.
That could be assumed, because after all there were fruits in paradise; if the apple was hanging on the tree, it must have been autumn. .
There's some truth to that.
But immediately another thought comes to his mind:
What kind of argument is that?
Could not the almighty God create such meager fruits extra, at any time of the year?
When they reach the main road leading to Rohatyn, they join the stream of pedestrians, horse riders and all kinds of wagons that emerge from the fog, like Christmas bread figures.
It's Wednesday, market day in Rohatyn, peasant carts loaded with sacks of grain, crates of poultry, all sorts of farm produce are going.
Between them march lively traders with every possible product.

Their little stalls, cleverly folded now, are carried on their backs like yokes, and in moments become tables full of colorful materials, wooden toys, eggs bought up in villages for a quarter of the price. .
The peasants also bring goats and cows to sell, the terrified animals resisting in the puddles amidst the clamor.
A speeding cart, covered with a threadbare tarp and full of noisy Jews heading to the Rohatyn fair from all around, passes them by.
Behind them, a wealthy carriage is struggling to maintain its dignity amidst the fog and bustle on the road.

Its clearly lacquered doors are blackened with mud, and the footman in his blue cape appears disconcerted he apparently did not anticipate such turmoil and is now desperately looking for an opportunity to get off this devilish road.
